analysis.one_liner: Bans most overdraft fees and caps the rest at one per month for bank customers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Banking Committee after one hearing and died when the Congress ended with 3 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would sharply limit overdraft fees, which banks charge when a customer spends more than the balance in their account. It would ban overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases altogether, cap fees on checks and recurring payments at one per month and six per year, require fees to be proportional to the bank's actual cost, ban nonsufficient-fund fees on debit card transactions, and require banks to stop reporting paid overdrafts to credit bureaus. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held a hearing but never voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Checking-account customers who occasionally overdraw — disproportionately low- and moderate-income households living paycheck to paycheck — would pay fewer and smaller overdraft fees, get clear disclosures and same-day notice when an overdraft happens, and avoid credit-report damage from paid overdrafts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Checking-account customers living paycheck to paycheck

how_it_helps.text: Bans overdraft coverage fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card transactions, the transactions that generate most overdraft fees; fees would remain only for checks and automatic recurring payments, and only with the customer's written consent.

Caps overdraft fees at one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account, and requires any fee to be reasonable and proportional to the bank's actual cost of covering the transaction, with a CFPB safe-harbor amount possible.
Banks could no longer charge a fee when an overdraft results only from a debit hold larger than the actual purchase amount, a practice that triggers fees for money the customer never actually spent.

Banks could not charge nonsufficient-fund fees on ATM or debit card transactions, and banks would have to post transactions in the order that minimizes fees rather than in the order that maximizes them.

Requires clear fee disclosures in marketing, same-day notice when an overdraft happens, itemized fee totals on monthly statements, and bans reporting negative information to credit bureaus for overdrafts repaid under an overdraft program, including deletion of past reports.

analysis.who_pays: Depository institutions — banks and credit unions — that collect overdraft and nonsufficient-fund fees, a multi-billion-dollar revenue stream concentrated at the largest banks, would bear the cost in the form of lost fee income and new disclosure, notice, and record-keeping requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and credit unions collecting overdraft fees

drawbacks.text: Banks argue overdraft fees fund the service of covering shortfalls and fraud losses, so eliminating them on most transactions would remove a service many customers use, and banks might respond by closing accounts for repeat overdrafters or raising other fees and minimum-balance requirements to make up the revenue.

The bill leaves overdraft fees in place for checks and recurring payments, so customers who overdraw mainly on those items would still face fees, and a CFPB rulemaking process would be needed to set the 'reasonable and proportional' standard before the full limits took practical effect.

The bill's findings assert that high flat fees fall hardest on low- and moderate-income consumers, but it would not cap the remaining fees at a specific dollar amount, instead relying on regulators to define proportionality.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is direct and one-sided: the households hit hardest by overdraft fees are those least able to absorb them, and the bill targets exactly those fees while keeping coverage available for checks and recurring payments at a capped, cost-based price. The real cost falls on banks' fee revenue, and the serious risk is that banks substitute other fees or account closings, which the bill addresses only partially through its nondiscrimination provision. A fair reading is that the bill trades bank fee income for consumer protections with modest regulatory burden, but its effectiveness would have depended heavily on CFPB rules defining 'reasonable and proportional.'

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee after a single hearing and never came up for a vote before the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 9, 2021 by Sen. Booker with Sen. Warren and was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
The committee held a hearing on May 4, 2022 but never held a markup or vote on the bill.
The bill ended with three cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Senate vote before the 117th Congress expired on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The banks and credit unions that collect overdraft and nonsufficient-fund fees are better off, because the fee restrictions never advanced. Checking-account customers who overdraw see no change from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks that collect overdraft fees

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by Democrats with three Democratic cosponsors and died in a Democratic-led committee without a markup or vote, so no recorded position for most members of either party.

industries.industry: Retail banks and other depository institutions
industries.note: Overdraft and nonsufficient-fund fees are a multi-billion-dollar revenue stream, concentrated at the largest banks and drawn mostly from customers who overdraw. The bill would cut deeply into that income by banning fees on ATM and debit card overdrafts, capping fees on checks and recurring payments at one per month, and requiring fees to match the bank's actual cost.
The bill would bar banks from reporting paid overdrafts to credit bureaus and would require deletion of old negative overdraft entries once repaid, shrinking the data these agencies hold.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would be required to write implementing rules within two years and could set a safe-harbor fee level, expanding its rulemaking role in consumer banking.
